payload.outcome: Superseded by E-996, which landed the same fix on 2026-05-01 (b7f12cb). payload.title: Announce a truncated list instead of cutting it off silently
payload.description: A list that gets cut off says nothing about it. `endless sql` and the listing verbs return every matching row with no cap, so a consumer that cannot predict the result size bounds it downstream with `head` — and `head` is silent, which makes a truncated result indistinguishable from a complete one. That silence turned two searches in one session into false "no existing task" conclusions: E-1935 fell off a `head -30` and E-1535 off a `head -24`, both ordered by id ASC so the newest and most relevant rows were exactly the ones dropped. Endless already has the right idiom — the session-status view never hides silently, printing "… N hidden (--show-hidden)". Give the listing surfaces a default cap that announces itself the same way, so the cap lives in the tool and describes itself instead of living in a pipe that cannot. Which commands need it is for the implementor to determine and confirm with the user.
payload.analysis:
## The precedent to copy

`internal/sessionstatuscmd/session_status.go` builds the footer:

    return fmt.Sprintf("… %d hidden (--show-hidden)", n)

E-1914 established the rule behind it — the view "never hides silently" — and
that is exactly the property the listing surfaces lack. This task applies the
existing idiom to result-set truncation rather than inventing one.

## Why more flags would not have fixed it

`task search` already has `--limit` (E-864), and it did not help. The cap that
bit was in the CALLER's pipe, not in the command, because the caller could not
predict the result size and so bounded it defensively. A cap that the tool owns
and announces removes the reason to reach for `head` at all; a flag the caller
must remember to pass does not.

## Recommended shape, for the implementor to confirm

- A default row cap on human-readable renders, with a footer naming what was
  dropped and how to see it, e.g. "… 47 more rows (--limit 0)".
- `--limit 0` (or `--all`) means no cap. Whatever spelling the surrounding
  commands already use wins over inventing a new one.
- MACHINE-READABLE formats are the trap. Silently capping a `--json`, `--llm` or
  `--tsv` payload would be strictly worse than today's problem: a consumer
  parsing 50 of 200 rows has no footer to read and no way to notice. Either
  leave those uncapped, or carry the truncation in the payload itself
  (`"truncated": true, "total": N`) so it is impossible to miss. Do not emit a
  human footer into a machine format.
- `endless sql` is the raw escape hatch and the one I actually truncate most.
  It deserves the cap even though — maybe because — it is the least structured
  surface.

## Evidence, from the session that filed this

Two false negatives, same mechanism, hours apart:

- Searching for an owning epic before filing rebuild work: `head -30`, ordered
  by id ASC, hid E-1935 (an epic that already owned the area). Three tasks were
  filed under the wrong parent as a result and had to be moved.
- Searching for existing work on a pre-completed status: `head -24`, ordered by
  id ASC, hid E-1535 and E-1663. A design question was reported to the user as
  settled when an existing task contradicted it.

Both were ordered ascending, so truncation removed the newest rows — and
recency is the relevance signal here, since recently filed tasks get attention
that months-old ones do not.

# Scope extension — the false-UNLANDED case (added 2026-08-10)

E-1940 covers two defects in `UnsettledDetail.Unsettled()`. There is a third,
opposite one, in the same function, and it has a second consumer.

## The defect

`internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go:172` runs
`git rev-list main..HEAD --count` and treats any non-zero result as unlanded.
Because `worktree land` REBASES onto main, a landed branch's commits are
rewritten — the originals stay on the branch and are unreachable from main by
construction. So every correctly-landed worktree reads "unlanded" forever, and
the count grows without bound as main advances.

Observed on E-1845: `task unsettled` reported "unlanded (161 commits)" for a
task that landed on 2026-08-05. Its commit IS on main as 2776f5a5 (same subject,
different SHA from the branch's ed41f1d2); the branch's merge-base with main is
1005 commits back. Most of the 161 were never E-1845's work at all — they were
main's commits at worktree-creation time, since rewritten.

This is worse than a wrong label: the printed fix is
`endless worktree land E-NNNN`, which would replay 161 stale commits onto a main
that already has the content.

## Second consumer — likely the worktree-backlog cause

`internal/monitor/reap_worktrees.go:220` runs the identical probe as reap
criterion 4. Criterion 1 already requires a `task_landings` row. So a landed
worktree passes 1 and is rejected by 4 — it can never be reaped, and landed
worktrees accumulate indefinitely.

## The fix

`task_landings` already records the landing (task_id, merge_commit_sha,
landed_at) and is already read by the reaper. Consult it before the rev-list
verdict: a task with a landing row whose recorded sha is reachable from main is
landed, whatever the branch's SHA divergence says.

Note that `git branch --merged main` does NOT work here — a rebase-landed branch
is not an ancestor of main. E-1308 proposes that probe for a related case and
would hit the same wall; the recorded landing is the reliable signal for both.

Verify with a rebase-landed worktree: `unsettled` must report settled, the ◆
marker must clear, and the reaper must consider it reapable.

# Consolidated from E-1308 (declined 2026-08-10)

E-1308 was a third symptom of this same cause. Its case: `worktree land E-NNNN`
when the worktree is GONE reports "No endless-managed worktree for E-NNN",
implying the work is lost. It isn't — the branch landed and the reaper later
removed the directory and branch once the `task_landings` row aged past
worktree_ttl.

Required behavior, carried over verbatim: report
"E-NNN already landed (commit <sha>); nothing to do" instead of the error, and
fall back to today's message only when the work is genuinely unaccounted for.

E-1308 proposed detecting this with `git branch --merged main`. That does not
work: `land` rebases, so a landed branch is not an ancestor of main and the
probe fails for exactly the case it targets. The recorded landing is the only
reliable signal — the same fix the unsettled probe and the reaper need.

## The three consumers, one primitive

| Consumer | Current probe | Symptom |
|---|---|---|
| `worktree_unsettled.go:172` | `rev-list main..HEAD --count` | false "unlanded (N commits)" forever after landing |
| `reap_worktrees.go:220` | same | landed worktrees never reaped; they accumulate |
| `worktree land` (gone worktree) | none / proposed `branch --merged` | "No endless-managed worktree", implying work lost |

Build the landed-state determination once — a task with a `task_landings` row
whose recorded sha is reachable from main is landed, regardless of branch SHA
divergence — and route all three through it.

payload.outcome: Consolidated into E-1940 per ED-1550 (3): several symptoms of one cause are one task. E-1308, the unsettled probe's false verdicts, and the reaper's refusal to reap landed worktrees are all the same defect — no reliable landed-state determination, so each surface invents its own git probe and all of them break on rebase-landed branches. E-1940 now owns the cause and carries E-1308's use-case verbatim in its analysis: report 'already landed (commit <sha>); nothing to do' when the worktree is gone, falling back to today's error only when the work is genuinely unaccounted for. Note for whoever implements it: E-1308's proposed 'git branch --merged main' probe does NOT work, because land rebases and a landed branch is therefore not an ancestor of main; the recorded task_landings row is the reliable signal.

E-1817 is the case in point: its outcome went through five rounds of Mike's correction after the session had already marked it completed, and each round materially changed the deliverable. Add `unreviewed` between `underway` and `completed` for these types, meaning "outcome written, awaiting the owner's read", so a self-declared finish is not the last word. fields.analysis:
Resolution of the open question the description carried, decided by Mike 2026-08-25: the new status is `unreviewed`.

WHY DISTINCT, NOT A REUSE OF `unverified`

`unverified` means "implementation done, awaiting verification", and research/epic/brainstorm are explicitly REFUSED it — E-1577/E-1579/ED-1516 gate it as a type-correctness invariant with no --force bypass, on the grounds that those types produce information rather than testable behavior and terminate via `completed --outcome`. That gate now lives in taskstatus.VerificationTrack. Reusing the lane would collapse a distinction those tasks deliberately drew, and would mean unpicking a hard gate three tasks built on purpose.

`unreviewed` says something different from `unverified` and the difference is the point: not "does it work" but "has the owner read it". E-1817 failed the second, never the first.

WHY ONE STATUS FOR BOTH TYPES

Brainstorm and research differ in deliverable — a synthesis versus findings — but not in the failure mode. Both finish on the author's say-so with nobody downstream. One name, one gate. If they later need to diverge, that is a membership change in one map, not a second status.

WHAT IT COSTS NOW THAT E-1891 HAS LANDED

This is the first status added since the registry exists, so it is also the first real test of whether E-1891 did its job. The mechanics: add the const to internal/taskstatus, and the single `groups` map forces a decision on every grouping rather than letting one be missed — which is the failure that hit E-1648 and E-1845. Three partition invariants fail until those decisions are made (actionable|not-actionable, children-state-order|terminal, and the four session-status dispositions), plus the label/glyph and membership-pinning tests. Python needs no vocabulary change at all: statuses.py holds nothing and reads whatever Go says.

The design work that remains is real and is why this stays `unplanned`: which groups `unreviewed` joins (in particular whether it blocks dependents the way `unverified` does), which surfaces render it, and how existing `completed` research/brainstorm rows are treated — left alone, most likely, since they already shipped.

# E-2018 — Enforce the documented status lifecycle on `task update`

## The defect

`task update --status` accepts any status from any status, from any actor,
whether or not a session ever claimed the task. Observed 2026-08-20: a session
holding E-1817 set E-2015 to `unverified` — a task that was `unplanned`, had
never been claimed, and had no worktree, so `session goto E-2015` found nothing
to go to. Both missing checks were computable from data Endless already had.

The lifecycle is byte-synced across three documents by a test while nothing
checks the lifecycle itself.

## Design: the Go table is the source, the diagram is generated

Not parsing `docs/status-lifecycle.mmd`. Parsing is deterministic — the
`stateDiagram-v2` transition syntax is a tiny regular subset and one regex
extracted every edge on the first try — but it makes a hand-authored document
load-bearing, and the diagram cannot express two axes the guard needs (which
actor may take an edge, and which task types a lane applies to).

Invert it. A transition table in `internal/taskstatus` is the source;
`docs/status-lifecycle.mmd` becomes a generated artifact. Drift stops being
something a test detects and becomes something that cannot happen.

This is not a new mechanism. `just guide-index` already regenerates a block
between `<!-- BEGIN generated: ... -->` / `<!-- END generated -->` markers and
`just guide-check` exits non-zero on drift as a pre-land gate. Same shape here.

**Generate the states and edges, not the whole file.** The editorial preamble
stays hand-written in the template — the same split `guide-index` uses.

## Step 0 — `blocked` leaves the vocabulary

`blocked` is not a status. It once was, and a handful of rows still carry it,
which is stale data rather than evidence of a design. Blockedness is the
`blocked_by` relation, computed from the blocker's own status — the guide's
blocking-semantics table has always described it that way, and `endless task
block` has only ever written a relation.

ED-1572 proposed writing this down and was rejected because it needs no
decision: "we need to clean up the data." That cleanup is nearly finished — one
row remains, E-627, whose own title records that E-891 superseded it, so
`task replace E-627 --by E-891` retires it.

So this task does not give `blocked` edges, in or out. It removes it:

- the `Blocked` constant and every group membership in `internal/taskstatus`
  (`All`, `ClaimPromotes`, `ChildrenStateOrder`, `SessionPending`,
  `StickyOverride`) — E-1891 relocated those faithfully, but faithful to a
  vocabulary that should not have contained it;
- the session-status disposition bucket keyed on it;
- its row in the guide's status table and the `--status` help text, both of
  which fall out for free once the vocabulary shrinks;
- `classify()`'s handling in `sessionstatuscmd`, which routes it today.

E-1891's partition invariants make this cheap to get right: remove the constant
and the tests name every group that still references it.

**Do this first and separately.** It is a vocabulary change, not a lifecycle
change, and mixing it into the table's first draft would make the diff
unreadable.

## Step 1 — the transition table

In `internal/taskstatus`, alongside the groups:

```go
type Transition struct {
    From, To Status
    Actor    Actor      // User, Agent, Session, System
    Types    []tasktype.TaskType  // empty = every type
    Label    string     // rendered as the mermaid edge label
}
```

Two columns the current diagram cannot carry:

- **Actor.** Today the diagram encodes it as prose in edge labels — "user
  approves", "session claims", "agent submits", "triage routes". Consistent
  enough to be a grammar, but a grammar in a picture is a DSL wearing mermaid
  syntax. Make it a column; the labels are then *rendered from* it, so the
  prose can no longer disagree with the rule.
- **Type.** `unverified → confirmed` is the implementation lane; `→ completed`
  is research and brainstorm (ED-1502). E-2016 adds `unreviewed` to that second
  lane. One diagram, several lifecycles.

**Deterministic order.** Go map iteration is randomized and the generated file
must be byte-stable, so the table is an ordered structure — `dtx.OrderedMap`
from `github.com/mikeschinkel/go-dt/dtx`, already a dependency. Order it to
*read* well — entry, happy path, reopening, terminal — not alphabetically.

**Two gaps the current diagram has, closed here.** `completed` has no inbound
edge at all, though research tasks land there and E-1817 itself is `completed` —
a diagram-derived guard would have refused the transition that closed the task
that filed this one. Write its inbound edges in. (The other gap was `blocked`,
handled in step 0.)

## Step 2 — the generator and its drift check

`endless-go task-status transitions` emits the table, mirroring the one-verb-per-
function shape E-1891 established. A `lifecycle-index` recipe renders
`docs/status-lifecycle.mmd` from it and re-syncs the two byte-copies in
`README.md` and `docs/guide/index.md`; `lifecycle-check` exits non-zero on drift
and joins the pre-land gate next to `guide-check`.

`tests/test_status_lifecycle_sync.py` does not go away — its job narrows. It
stops asserting that three hand-maintained copies match each other and starts
asserting that the committed artifact is current: the `gofmt -l` shape.

## Step 3 — the guard

Two checks, both at `execTaskFieldsUpdated` in `internal/events/executor.go` —
the same executor and the same route that let E-2067's parent cycle through.

Follow `ValidateNoParentCycle` exactly (landed in 320c375): a plain exported
validator in the `events` package, called from the executor when the write
actually touches the field. E-2067 chose a shared function over a registry;
follow it rather than inventing a second arrangement. Note the asymmetry —
E-2067's guard needs only the tasks table, while this one needs the transition
table, so the hook is shared but the data behind it is not.

**Transition legality.** `ValidateStatusTransition(from, to, taskType)` refuses
an edge absent from the table. The message names the illegal edge and lists the
statuses that ARE reachable from the current one, so the caller's next move is
in the refusal rather than in the docs.

**Actor reality.** A session may not set `underway` or `unverified` on a task it
does not hold, and `unverified` requires that some session claimed the task at
some point — `sessions.task_id` is write-once (ED-1560), so that is a lookup,
not a heuristic. A caller with no session at all (a human at a terminal, cron,
a migration) is exempt: this guards against an agent's mistake, not against a
person, and `actor_kind` already distinguishes them.

### Enforcement: refuse, with no `--force`

Following E-1577/E-1579's precedent for the type×status gate — a correctness
invariant with no bypass, on the grounds that the fix is to correct the call,
not to override the gate. A `--force` here would be reached for on the first
missing edge and would become habit, and an override that becomes habit is a
guard that has stopped meaning anything.

The risk this accepts is a legal-but-unwritten edge stranding someone until a
fix lands. Two things make that tolerable: the table is authored fresh rather
than derived from the incomplete diagram, and step 2 renders the diagram FROM
it, so a missing edge is visible in the picture everyone already reads rather
than hidden in a Go literal.

## Sequencing

Step 0, then 1, then 2, then 3 — and steps 0 and 3 are separately landable, so
the vocabulary fix does not wait on the generator.

E-2016 (`unreviewed`) is blocked on this and should stay that way: if this lands
first, `unreviewed` adds two edges to an existing graph instead of arriving with
no enforcement to hook into.

## Verification

Split by durability, per E-1889's convention.

**Real suites — permanent invariants:**

- Go, `taskstatus`: every transition's `From`/`To` are in the vocabulary (the
  subset invariant E-1891 already runs, extended to the table); the table is
  connected — every status is reachable from `untriaged` and every non-terminal
  status has an outbound edge, so a status cannot be added and stranded; the
  rendered order is byte-stable across runs.
- Go, the guard: each refused edge refuses and each legal edge passes, walked
  over the table rather than hand-listed; the actor rules; and the exemption for
  a caller with no session.
- Go, the generator: rendering twice gives identical bytes, and the check verb
  fails on a hand-edited artifact.
- pytest: the two byte-copies match the canonical file (narrowed from the
  current test), and `task update --status` surfaces the refusal as a clean CLI
  error rather than a traceback.

**`tests/tasks/e-2018-verify.sh` — acceptance.** Harness shape from
`tests/tasks/e-1891-verify.sh`, fail-fast section A, project-wide regression
last. It asserts: the reported case refuses end-to-end (`task update <unplanned,
never-claimed> --status unverified` is rejected, naming the reachable
statuses); `blocked` is gone from the vocabulary and from every group; the
generated diagram is current; and a legal path — file, submit, approve, claim,
finish — still runs unimpeded.

## Explicitly not in scope

- Enforcing the lifecycle on any writer other than `task update`. The other
  status writers (`task submit`, `approve`, `claim`, `confirm`) each already
  encode their own single legal edge; routing them through the table is a
  simplification, not a fix, and belongs in its own task.
- Transitive block computation across `blocked_by` chains — that is E-1553.

payload.text:
# Make the worktree-removal prohibition categorical in the handoff templates

## Context

Every spawned session's handoff carries this rule:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop` without asking.

That form asks the session to evaluate a precondition — *have I been asked?* —
and that evaluation is where it fails. On 2026-08-25 two separate sessions
destroyed worktrees within ten minutes of each other. Neither overrode the rule.
Both concluded the precondition was satisfied by conversational text that did not
satisfy it (in one case, "if it can be reaped, you don't need to tell me about
it" — a remark about what is worth reporting, read as authorization to act). One
of the two caused real damage.

`land` and `drop` do not deserve the same rule. Landing is the normal end of a
task and the spawning session owns the timing, so "ask first" is right. Removal
is destructive, is never part of finishing a task, and has no benign case a
spawned session needs. It should carry no precondition at all.

## The change

Six templates carry the line. Five share the numbered form:

    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/todo.md.tmpl        line 16
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/bugfix.md.tmpl      line 18
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/research.md.tmpl    line 16
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/brainstorm.md.tmpl  line 18
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/epic.md.tmpl        line 27

Replace, in each:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop` without asking.

with:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land` without asking. NEVER remove a
       worktree — not `endless worktree drop`, not `endless worktree reap`,
       not `git worktree remove`. The spawning session owns removal. If
       removal looks warranted, say so once and stop.

The sixth is inline mid-sentence and needs its own edit rather than a blind
substitution:

    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/claim.md.tmpl       line 19

    ... STOP and ask. Don't guess. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop`
    without asking.

becomes:

    ... STOP and ask. Don't guess. Don't run `endless worktree land` without
    asking, and NEVER remove a worktree — not `endless worktree drop`, not
    `endless worktree reap`, not `git worktree remove`.

Naming three commands rather than one is deliberate: a `drop`-only prohibition
is satisfiable by reaching for `git worktree remove`, which is the same outcome
by another route. The rule has to name the outcome.

Check `_mechanics.tmpl` and `_close.tmpl` for a copy of the same sentence before
finishing — the five numbered files were found by grep for "worktree land", and a
paraphrase would not have matched.

## The materialization trap — do not miss this

`endless-go template` resolves each template in this order (see the package
comment in internal/templatecmd/template.go):

    1. <project_root>/.endless/templates/<name>.local.tmpl   per-developer
    2. <project_root>/.endless/templates/<name>.tmpl         committed
    3. embedded                                              fallback

The committed copy is materialized from embed **on first render**. This project
currently has zero materialized handoff templates, so editing the embedded files
is sufficient here — but confirm that is still true at implementation time:

    ls .endless/templates/

If a materialized `handoff/*.tmpl` exists, it wins over the embedded edit and
must be updated too, or the fix silently does nothing.

PRODUCT: an adopting project that has already rendered a handoff has a
materialized copy carrying the old, weaker rule, and a version upgrade will not
change it. Their sessions keep the conditional wording indefinitely. Decide
whether that is acceptable (say so in the outcome) or whether it needs its own
task — do not solve it here.

## Test

No test asserts the current wording, which is why it could have been reworded or
dropped silently. Add one so the rule cannot regress. `internal/templatecmd/`
already has the right shape in claim_handoff_test.go (TestRender_Claim_* render
a handoff and assert on its content). Add a test that renders each task type's
handoff and asserts the rendered text contains "NEVER remove a worktree" and does
NOT contain "land`/`drop` without asking".

Assert against the RENDERED output, not the file bytes, so the test also covers
the claim path and any future template that grows a copy of the rule.

## Verification

Fold into `tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh` as a fail-fast unit gate plus:

1. `go test ./internal/templatecmd/` passes, including the new test.
2. Rendering a handoff for each of the five task types shows the new rule and no
   occurrence of the old sentence.
3. `just test` and `just test-go` pass project-wide.

## Out of scope

A PreToolUse hook that blocks worktree removal at the tool layer. That is the
durable fix — this one is prose a session chooses to honor, and two sessions in
one evening chose not to. Mike has been told; it is his call whether to file it.
Do not build it here, and do not file it without asking.

# Plan

Three landable increments. Each leaves the tree green and shippable; do not
start the next until the previous has landed.

## Increment 1 — the tables, written but not yet authoritative

New schema change file `internal/schema/changes/e-2063-session-instances.sql`,
mirrored into `internal/schema/schema.sql`.

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS session_instances (
    id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    session_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sessions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    harness       TEXT    NOT NULL,
    first_seen_at TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S','now')),
    last_event_at TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S','now')),
    ended_at      TEXT,
    recap         TEXT,
    recap_through TEXT,
    UNIQUE (id, harness)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS claude_cli_sessions (
    instance_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    harness     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (harness = 'claude_cli'),
    uuid        TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    FOREIGN KEY (instance_id, harness)
        REFERENCES session_instances (id, harness)
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS session_instances_by_session
    ON session_instances (session_id, first_seen_at);
```

NO `UNIQUE (session_id) WHERE ended_at IS NULL`. `ended_at` is display-only —
see the analysis; adding that index re-opens a settled decision.

Backfill in the same change file: one instance per existing `sessions` row,
`first_seen_at` from `sessions.started_at`, `last_event_at` from
`sessions.last_activity`, `harness` from `sessions.platform`, `ended_at` set
when `state='ended'`, and a `claude_cli_sessions` row carrying
`sessions.session_id` where that is non-empty and `platform='claude'`.

Nothing reads the new tables yet. Land here.

## Increment 2 — resolution moves to the instance

`sessions.session_id` stays in place and keeps being written, so this increment
is reversible; it stops being the resolution key, not the stored value.

- `monitor.GetActiveSession(uuid)` resolves uuid -> `claude_cli_sessions` ->
  `session_instances` -> `sessions`, returning the Endless session.
- `monitor.TouchSession` upserts the INSTANCE (bumping `last_event_at`, clearing
  a stale `ended_at`), and upserts the `sessions` row only when no instance
  matches the uuid.
- SessionStart: when the window/task already has a session and the uuid is new,
  append an instance rather than inserting a `sessions` row. `payload.Source`
  (`startup`/`resume`/`clear`/`compact`) is currently read nowhere; read it here
  and treat anything other than `startup` as continuation.
- Close the prior instance (`ended_at`) when a clear appends a new one.
- `session_messages.session_id` FKs `sessions(session_id)` — the uuid, not the
  id. Re-point it at `session_instances.id` so a clear gives later transcript
  rows a new parent and no prior row is rewritten.
- Move `platform` off `sessions`; `session_instances.harness` is the single
  discriminator.

## The governing rule

**Any field that is a fact about the unique harness conversation moves to
`session_instances`. Anything that is a fact about the WORK stays on
`sessions`.** Applied to rows as well as columns, that is the whole migration —
and it is why keeping the FIRST `sessions.id` of a set loses nothing: once the
conversation-specific columns have moved, the surviving row holds only facts
that were never conversation-specific to begin with.

Columns that MOVE to the instance:

| column              | becomes                              |
|---------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `session_id` (uuid) | `claude_cli_sessions.uuid`           |
| `platform`          | `session_instances.harness`          |
| `started_at`        | `session_instances.first_seen_at`    |
| `last_activity`     | `session_instances.last_event_at`    |
| `state`             | per-conversation                     |
| `process_id`        | the process running THIS conversation|
| `transcript_offset` | how far THIS transcript is parsed    |
| `summary`           | per-conversation                     |
| `last_user_prompt`  | per-turn, so per-conversation        |
| `report_bounces`    | per-turn                             |
| `report_exempt`     | per-turn                             |
| `report_runs`       | per-turn                             |

Columns that STAY on `sessions`: `id`, `project_id`, `task_id`, `epic_id`,
`hidden`. These describe the work and its durable identity, and must survive a
clear.

Four columns are NOT classified here because they will not exist: `summary`,
`short_id`, `kind_id` and `plan_file_path` are removed by E-2074, which blocks
this task. `kind_id` takes the `session_kinds` table and its Go enum with it.
The instance gets `recap` / `recap_through`; `summary` is not carried over.

The same rule decides the referencing tables. Per-conversation rows follow their
conversation to its instance: `session_messages` (transcripts), `session_gates`
(relay checkpoints and the minimizer corpus triples — both per-turn),
`report_labels`, `session_navigations`. Per-session rows stay pointed at the
surviving `sessions.id`: `session_tasks`, `decisions.origin_session_id`,
`task_landings`, `project_next_events`.

Getting the per-conversation direction wrong is the failure that matters:
re-pointing those rows at the surviving session would flatten every prior
conversation into one and destroy exactly the history this redesign exists to
preserve.

## Increment 3 — the collapse, and the CLI

- Re-parent the multiple `sessions` rows per task that exist today (E-1307 has
  7; 1362 and 1322 have 6). NOTHING IS DISCARDED: the earliest row by
  `started_at` remains the session, and every other row BECOMES AN INSTANCE of
  it, carrying its own uuid, timestamps and `ended_at`. Seven conversations stay
  seven conversations; they stop being seven sessions. Re-point the referencing
  tables per the split above — per-conversation rows follow their conversation
  to its instance, per-session rows follow the survivor.
- `resume` refuses when a session has 2+ instances with `ended_at IS NULL`:
  print them ordered by `first_seen_at` ASC with ordinal, `first_seen_at`,
  `last_event_at`, message count and recap, and exit non-zero. Never close one
  automatically. `--instance <ordinal|uuid>` selects.
- `resume` and `goto --resume` share ONE resolver.
- Delete `spawn --new-session`; under one-session-per-task it cannot mean what
  it says. OPEN, and NOT yet decided by the requester: whether its one
  legitimate residue — "do not inject the prior conversation's context into the
  handoff" — is still wanted at all, and if so under what name. Do not invent a
  flag for it without asking.
- Split `spawn --reopen` into `reopen` (task-status verb) and `resume` (session
  verb; restores the worktree, navigates when a live owner exists).

# Verification

`tests/tasks/e-2063-verify.sh`, fail-fast on units then end-to-end through the
real hook against the sandbox DB (drive it with an explicit `--config-dir`, per
`tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh` — without that flag the hook's PinMainDB sends
writes to the REAL ledger).

1. A clear appends: feed SessionStart with a NEW uuid and `source=clear` for a
   window whose session exists; assert exactly one `sessions` row for the task
   before and after, and one more `session_instances` row after.
2. Resume does not append: same, `source=resume` with the existing uuid; assert
   the instance count is unchanged.
3. The prior instance is closed on a clear; the surviving one has
   `ended_at IS NULL`.
4. A stale `ended_at` blocks nothing: leave two instances open, insert a third,
   assert it succeeds. This is the regression guard on the rejected index.
5. `resume` with 2+ open instances exits non-zero, lists them ordered by
   `first_seen_at` ASC, and closes nothing — assert `ended_at` values are
   identical before and after.
6. `--instance` selects by both ordinal and uuid.
7. A `claude_cli_sessions` row cannot attach to a non-`claude_cli` instance —
   assert the composite FK rejects it.
8. Migration preserves history, asserted as a conservation law rather than a
   row count: for each task, `COUNT(session_instances)` after == `COUNT(sessions)`
   before, and every pre-migration uuid is still reachable. Then per-conversation
   rows: no `session_gates` / `session_messages` / `report_labels` row may end up
   parented to an instance whose uuid differs from the session uuid it had
   before. That is the assertion that catches a flattening migration; a bare
   pre/post row count would not.
9. `sessions.platform` is gone and nothing references it.

Not verifiable by test: whether one open instance per session is actually
maintained in the field. Nothing enforces it at the storage layer by design —
that is E-1983's invariant gate plus write-once `task_id`.

# Scope extension — the false-UNLANDED case (added 2026-08-10)

E-1940 covers two defects in `UnsettledDetail.Unsettled()`. There is a third,
opposite one, in the same function, and it has a second consumer.

## The defect

`internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go:172` runs
`git rev-list main..HEAD --count` and treats any non-zero result as unlanded.
Because `worktree land` REBASES onto main, a landed branch's commits are
rewritten — the originals stay on the branch and are unreachable from main by
construction. So every correctly-landed worktree reads "unlanded" forever, and
the count grows without bound as main advances.

Observed on E-1845: `task unsettled` reported "unlanded (161 commits)" for a
task that landed on 2026-08-05. Its commit IS on main as 2776f5a5 (same subject,
different SHA from the branch's ed41f1d2); the branch's merge-base with main is
1005 commits back. Most of the 161 were never E-1845's work at all — they were
main's commits at worktree-creation time, since rewritten.

This is worse than a wrong label: the printed fix is
`endless worktree land E-NNNN`, which would replay 161 stale commits onto a main
that already has the content.

## Second consumer — likely the worktree-backlog cause

`internal/monitor/reap_worktrees.go:220` runs the identical probe as reap
criterion 4. Criterion 1 already requires a `task_landings` row. So a landed
worktree passes 1 and is rejected by 4 — it can never be reaped, and landed
worktrees accumulate indefinitely.

## The fix

`task_landings` already records the landing (task_id, merge_commit_sha,
landed_at) and is already read by the reaper. Credit it: the commits a recorded
landing accounts for are not unlanded, whatever the branch's SHA divergence
says.

Note that `git branch --merged <base>` does NOT work here — a rebase-landed
branch is not an ancestor of the base. E-1308 proposes that probe for a related
case and would hit the same wall; the recorded landing is the reliable signal
for both.

### Anchor the credit on the BRANCH, not on the base (revised 2026-08-25)

This section originally said: a task whose recorded sha is reachable from main
is landed. Measurement against this repo falsified that before implementation.

- Most recorded landing shas ARE reachable from main, but a substantial
  minority are not — main's own history has been rewritten more than once, and
  a rewrite detaches every landing recorded before it.
- E-1889, the case this analysis was written from, is one of them. NONE of its
  recorded shas is reachable from main, so the reachable-from-main rule would
  have left the motivating symptom exactly as broken as it found it.
- Every affected branch, without exception, still reaches its own recorded
  landing sha. The branch is the durable anchor; the base is not.

So the primitive is: **unlanded = the commits reachable from HEAD that are
reachable neither from the base branch nor from any recorded landing.**

    git rev-list --count --ignore-missing HEAD ^<base> ^<landing>...

Excluding the base as well as the landings is what keeps the count honest when
the base has moved on: it counts only commits that are genuinely this branch's
and genuinely not in. `--ignore-missing` covers a landing sha that is no longer
an object in this clone; it cannot mask a bad base, because the resolver only
ever returns a branch it verified exists.

Applied to the affected worktrees, every false count collapsed to zero while
the branches carrying real post-landing commits kept theirs.

Verify with a rebase-landed worktree: `unsettled` must report settled, the ◆
marker must clear, and the reaper must consider it reapable. Verify the
distinction that motivated the revision by rewriting the base's history
afterwards — the verdict must not move.

E-1308 was a third symptom of this same cause. Its case: `worktree land E-NNNN`
when the worktree is GONE reports "No endless-managed worktree for E-NNN",
implying the work is lost. It isn't — the branch landed and the reaper later
removed the directory and branch once the `task_landings` row aged past
worktree_ttl.

Required behavior, carried over verbatim: report

reliable signal — the same fix the unsettled probe and the reaper need.

whose recorded sha is reachable from main is landed, regardless of branch SHA
divergence — and route all three through it.

# E-1940 — Make the unsettled probe stop reporting "I could not tell" as "you are clear"

Absorbs E-1166. Decisions below are settled unless flagged OPEN.

## Problem

`UnsettledDetail.Unsettled()` returns false — the all-clear — whenever its git
probes could not run. The reaper runs the SAME two probes and already fails
closed ("Any git error while running 4 or 5 is treated as 'in use' — the reaper
would rather skip a candidate it can't reason about than destroy in-flight
work"). So the two surfaces the code claims agree on what "done and landed"
means actually diverge exactly where it matters, and the display picked the
unsafe polarity.

The hardcoded `main` is what makes this permanent rather than rare: on a repo
whose default branch differs, `git rev-list main..HEAD` exits 128 every time,
so `◆` can never appear and the reaper never reaps.

## Settled decisions

| # | Decision | Rejected alternative |
|---|----------|----------------------|
| 1 | Probe failure records a **fault** (E-698's system, already landed). | A new `?` glyph and legend entry. |
| 2 | Default branch resolved by one **shared helper**, used by the unsettled probe AND the reaper. | Fixing the display only and leaving the reaper on `main`. |
| 3 | E-1166 is **absorbed**: the Python `_default_base_branch` fix lands here too, under one strategy. | Two independent resolvers, one per language. |
| 4 | A probe failure marks the task's own row `◆`, alongside the fault. | Badge-only: `◆` keeps its narrow meaning and the row renders as if clean. |

## A. Shared default-branch resolver

New `monitor.DefaultBranch(repoDir) (string, error)`. Resolution order:

1. `.endless/config.json` `default_branch`, when set — explicit beats detection.
2. `git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, stripped of `origin/`.
3. `git config init.defaultBranch`.
4. Probe `main`, then `master`, for an existing local ref.
5. Otherwise a real error — the caller decides, and no caller may silently
   substitute `main`.

Step 2 is unset on fresh clones (it needs `git remote set-head`) — that is
E-1166's original finding and why steps 3–5 exist. Resolution is per-repo and
should be memoized for the process; `session monitor` calls the probe every 2s
per row and must not add a git call per row per tick.

## B. Call sites

- `internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go` — `worktreeUnsettledAt`'s probe 2.
- `internal/monitor/reap_worktrees.go` — `maybeReapWorktree` condition 4.
- `src/endless/worktree_cmd.py` — `_default_base_branch` (absorbed E-1166).

The Go and Python implementations must agree on the order above; assert that in
the tests rather than trusting prose.

## C. Polarity and reporting

`UnsettledDetail` gains an explicit undetermined state rather than overloading
the existing booleans:

- `Unsettled()` returns **true** when a probe failed, so the task's own row is
  marked. The alternative — report only in the badge and leave the row looking
  clean — was rejected: the row is the surface actually scanned, and a row that
  renders identically to a verified-clean one is the exact failure this task
  exists to remove. Marking the row is what tells you WHICH task is
  unverifiable without opening the fault.
- This widens `◆` from "you have work to land" to "look at this task — unlanded
  or uncheckable". That is a deliberate trade, and it is why the distinction
  below must be retrievable.
- `IsUndetermined()` reports it distinctly, so `task unsettled <id>` says which
  probe failed and why. `Reason()` already prints the error text today — that
  half is honest and stays. The list view collapses; the detail view explains.
- No new glyph, and no legend change beyond the fault badge E-698 already
  renders.

A fault is recorded on probe failure, so the condition is visible even when no
one is looking at that row, and is clearable. Faults are deduped by
fingerprint — key on (task id, failing probe) so a monitor ticking every 2s
raises one incident, not thousands.

## D. Fault codes

Two new entries in `internal/faults/codes.go` (numbers never reused; take the
next free ids):

- **worktree-probe-failed** — `git status` or `rev-list` failed for a worktree.
  Severity `error`: the user asked "is my work safe?" and Endless could not
  answer.
- **default-branch-unresolved** — resolution fell through every step in A.
  Severity `error`, same reasoning; it disables the probe entirely.

Both carry the task id, worktree path, failing command, and git's stderr in
`Fields`/`Detail`.

## E. Reaper

Condition 4 takes the resolver. Its fail-closed handling is already correct and
must not be touched. Fixing the branch resolution is what lets a non-`main`
project reap at all — today every candidate errors and is skipped forever.

This change touches the code path that DELETES worktrees, so the tests must pin
that a resolver error still yields "skip", never "reap".

## F. Landed state comes from the recorded landing

Scope confirmed with Mike 2026-08-25: this task ships the analysis's half too,
because it lands in the same two call sites as A-E and splitting it would mean
one rewriting the other.

`worktree land` rebases before fast-forwarding, so a landed commit is rewritten
under a new SHA while the branch keeps the original. `<base>..HEAD` therefore
reports a correctly-landed branch as unlanded forever, the count growing as the
base advances, and the remedy it prints would replay stale commits. The same
probe is reap condition 4, which is why landed worktrees accumulate.

One primitive, three consumers:

- unlanded = commits reachable from HEAD, reachable neither from the base
  branch nor from any recorded landing
  (`rev-list --count --ignore-missing HEAD ^<base> ^<landing>...`).
- The unsettled probe and the reaper both build their range through it, so
  they cannot disagree about what "landed" means.
- `worktree land` on a task whose worktree is gone consults the recorded
  landing and reports "already landed (commit <sha>)" instead of implying the
  work is lost. Absorbs E-1308.

The credit anchors on the BRANCH, not on the base: a recorded sha is excluded
from the branch's own history. Reachability from the base was the analysis's
original proposal and was falsified by measurement before implementation — a
rewrite of the base detaches every landing recorded before it, including every
one belonging to the case the analysis was written from. The analysis records
the revision and the evidence.

The path-based probe resolves landings best-effort from the `e-NNNN` directory
name. That softens E-1766's DB-free rule rather than reversing it: the lookup is
never authoritative, every failure is silent, and a miss only returns the count
to its pre-E-1940 over-reporting. Python threads its resolved `--config-dir` to
the Go subprocess so `--db main` renders a verdict computed against the same
database the caller is reading.

## Verification

**Durable tests** (these outlive the task):

- Go: resolver returns each step's answer in order, and errors rather than
  defaulting to `main` when all fail; `Unsettled()` is true on `StatusErr` and
  on `RevListErr`; `IsUndetermined()` separates that from real unsettled work;
  a fault is recorded once per (task, probe) rather than per tick; the reaper
  skips on resolver error.
- pytest: the Python resolver agrees with the Go order.
- A `master`-based fixture repo: `◆` appears for genuinely unlanded work and
  the reaper can reap. This is the regression that proves the product works
  outside `main`.
- The landing credit: a rebase-landed branch reads settled; a commit made AFTER
  the landing still reads unlanded; and rewriting the base's history afterwards
  does not move either verdict.

**`tests/tasks/e-1940-verify.sh`** — acceptance. **Author a script, NOT a
`.endless/tasks/e-1940/verify.toml`**: the manifest form is not the norm until
the verification-suite epic lands.

## Absorbed

- **E-1166** — absorbed; mark obsolete with an outcome naming this task.

## Not in scope

Local-vs-remote divergence (unpushed commits, `origin/main` ahead/behind).
`session status` answers "is this worktree's work landed into main?" — landing
is a local rebase + fast-forward, so LOCAL `main` is the correct reference and
the current comparison is right.

# Make the worktree-removal prohibition categorical in the handoff templates

## Context

Every spawned session's handoff carries this rule:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop` without asking.

That form asks the session to evaluate a precondition — *have I been asked?* —
and that evaluation is where it fails. On 2026-08-25 two separate sessions
destroyed worktrees within ten minutes of each other. Neither overrode the rule.
Both concluded the precondition was satisfied by conversational text that did not
satisfy it (in one case, "if it can be reaped, you don't need to tell me about
it" — a remark about what is worth reporting, read as authorization to act). One
of the two caused real damage.

`land` and `drop` do not deserve the same rule. Landing is the normal end of a
task and the spawning session owns the timing, so "ask first" is right. Removal
is destructive, is never part of finishing a task, and has no benign case a
spawned session needs. It should carry no precondition at all.

## The change

Six templates carry the line. Five share the numbered form:

    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/todo.md.tmpl        line 16
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/bugfix.md.tmpl      line 18
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/research.md.tmpl    line 16
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/brainstorm.md.tmpl  line 18
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/epic.md.tmpl        line 27

Replace, in each:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop` without asking.

with:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land` without asking. NEVER remove a
       worktree — not `endless worktree drop`, not `endless worktree reap`,
       not `git worktree remove`. The spawning session owns removal. If
       removal looks warranted, say so once and stop.

The sixth is inline mid-sentence and needs its own edit rather than a blind
substitution:

    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/claim.md.tmpl       line 19

    ... STOP and ask. Don't guess. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop`
    without asking.

becomes:

    ... STOP and ask. Don't guess. Don't run `endless worktree land` without
    asking, and NEVER remove a worktree — not `endless worktree drop`, not
    `endless worktree reap`, not `git worktree remove`.

Naming three commands rather than one is deliberate: a `drop`-only prohibition
is satisfiable by reaching for `git worktree remove`, which is the same outcome
by another route. The rule has to name the outcome.

finishing — the five numbered files were found by grep for "worktree land", and a
paraphrase would not have matched.

`endless-go template` resolves each template in this order (see the package
comment in internal/templatecmd/template.go):

    2. <project_root>/.endless/templates/<name>.tmpl         committed
    3. embedded                                              fallback

The committed copy is materialized from embed **on first render**. This project
currently has zero materialized handoff templates, so editing the embedded files
is sufficient here — but confirm that is still true at implementation time:

    ls .endless/templates/

If a materialized `handoff/*.tmpl` exists, it wins over the embedded edit and
must be updated too, or the fix silently does nothing.

dropped silently. Add one so the rule cannot regress. `internal/templatecmd/`
already has the right shape in claim_handoff_test.go (TestRender_Claim_* render
a handoff and assert on its content). Add a test that renders each task type's
handoff and asserts the rendered text contains "NEVER remove a worktree" and does
NOT contain "land`/`drop` without asking".

the claim path and any future template that grows a copy of the rule.

A PreToolUse hook that blocks worktree removal at the tool layer. That is the
durable fix — this one is prose a session chooses to honor, and two sessions in
one evening chose not to. Mike has been told; it is his call whether to file it.
Do not build it here, and do not file it without asking.

# Make the worktree-removal prohibition categorical in the handoff templates

## Context

Every spawned session's handoff carries this rule:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop` without asking.

That form asks the session to evaluate a precondition — *have I been asked?* —
and that evaluation is where it fails. On 2026-08-25 two separate sessions
destroyed worktrees within ten minutes of each other. Neither overrode the rule.
Both concluded the precondition was satisfied by conversational text that did not
satisfy it (in one case, "if it can be reaped, you don't need to tell me about
it" — a remark about what is worth reporting, read as authorization to act). One
of the two caused real damage.

`land` and `drop` do not deserve the same rule. Landing is the normal end of a
task and the spawning session owns the timing, so "ask first" is right. Removal
is destructive, is never part of finishing a task, and has no benign case a
spawned session needs. It should carry no precondition at all.

## The change

Six templates carry the line. Five share the numbered form:

    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/todo.md.tmpl        line 16
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/bugfix.md.tmpl      line 18
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/research.md.tmpl    line 16
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/brainstorm.md.tmpl  line 18
    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/epic.md.tmpl        line 27

Replace, in each:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop` without asking.

with:

    7. Don't run `endless worktree land` without asking. NEVER remove a
       worktree — not `endless worktree drop`, not `endless worktree reap`,
       not `git worktree remove`. The spawning session owns removal. If
       removal looks warranted, say so once and stop.

The sixth is inline mid-sentence and needs its own edit rather than a blind
substitution:

    internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/claim.md.tmpl       line 19

    ... STOP and ask. Don't guess. Don't run `endless worktree land`/`drop`
    without asking.

becomes:

    ... STOP and ask. Don't guess. Don't run `endless worktree land` without
    asking, and NEVER remove a worktree — not `endless worktree drop`, not
    `endless worktree reap`, not `git worktree remove`.

Naming three commands rather than one is deliberate: a `drop`-only prohibition
is satisfiable by reaching for `git worktree remove`, which is the same outcome
by another route. The rule has to name the outcome.

Check `_mechanics.tmpl` and `_close.tmpl` for a copy of the same sentence before
finishing — the five numbered files were found by grep for "worktree land", and a
paraphrase would not have matched.

## Scope of the edit

Edit the embedded templates only. Do not write to `.endless/templates/`.

## Test

No test asserts the current wording, which is why it could have been reworded or
dropped silently. Add one so the rule cannot regress. `internal/templatecmd/`
already has the right shape in claim_handoff_test.go (TestRender_Claim_* render
a handoff and assert on its content). Add a test that renders each task type's
handoff and asserts the rendered text contains "NEVER remove a worktree" and does
NOT contain "land`/`drop` without asking".

Assert against the RENDERED output, not the file bytes, so the test also covers
the claim path and any future template that grows a copy of the rule.

3. `just test` and `just test-go` pass project-wide.

payload.analysis:
## Why relocation, not just a stronger rule

The rule already exists and has been violated repeatedly. What makes it fragile
is that the scripts are shelved with a real test suite: `just test` runs
tests/, the scripts sit at tests/tasks/, and "check for regressions" reads as
"run what is under tests/". Nothing about the path says "these execute against
live state, one at a time, by the session that owns the task".

## What is actually unsafe

Relocation stops accidental sweeps. It does not stop a deliberate wrong run,
and it does not make the scripts safe. The underlying hazard is that some of
them reach the live environment at all:

- e-1202-verify pipes a synthetic payload into the real hook binary with no
  --config-dir and no XDG_CONFIG_HOME override, so the hook lazy-creates a
  session row in the main database and binds it to $TMUX_PANE.
- Others shell out to git, tmux and endless-go; how many are hermetic is
  unknown and worth measuring rather than assuming.

Newer scripts (e-2067, e-2071) build a throwaway config dir under the cache
sandbox root and run the CLI from outside the repo, so the pattern for a
hermetic fixture already exists in-tree and can be the model.

## Scope to settle before moving anything

- Where they land. `.verify/` keeps them near .endless/ and out of tests/;
  a sibling of tests/ that is not tests/ is the only hard requirement.
- Every reference that resolves a script by task id: the justfile, docs/guide,
  `endless verify`, the scripts' own "Run from inside the worktree" headers,
  and any spawn/handoff prose that names the path.
- Whether a guard belongs in the harness — refusing a bulk invocation outright
  beats relying on the reader to notice the directory changed.
- An audit of which scripts touch live state, and whether those should be made
  hermetic on the same pass or tracked separately.

fields.analysis:
## Why prose is not enough

The rule already exists and is unambiguous. It was read, understood, paraphrased into "not required", and broken — by a session that could quote it. An agent's compliance with prose is negotiable at the moment it is inconvenient, which is precisely the moment enforcement has to exist.

## The load-bearing fix: guard inside the script

Each script already resolves its worktree root via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` in `main()`. Add a guard there: ask endless which task this worktree holds and exit 2 unless it matches the script's own id, with a refusal that names the sanctioned runners (`endless verify <id>`, `just verify <id>`) rather than just saying no.

Put it in a shared helper the scripts source, not copied into each — there are ~40 scripts and a copied guard is ~40 chances to omit it. Add it to whatever template new scripts are written from so one authored next month inherits it. Both sanctioned runners already know the task id, so they pass by construction.

This layer works for every user, every harness, and a human at a shell prompt.

## Second symptom, same root cause

A landed script's source-shape greps go stale on legitimate refactors of code the script does not own. `e-1956-verify.sh` lines 155 and 161 grep for literal spellings — `!isTerminal(r.Status)` and a JOIN clause — that E-1185 has since factored away. The properties they stood for are intact and now pinned by behavioral tests on both sides (`TestReplacedByNote_TerminalGate`, `test_replaced_by_map_ignores_a_removed_replacement`, and their duplicates counterparts).

Under prose-only rules that stale grep is a landmine: the next refactorer runs it, sees red, and "fixes" working code to match — which is exactly what happened here. Under the guard it is inert, because nobody outside E-1956's worktree can reach it. One cause, two symptoms, one task.

## Optional second layer, not a substitute

A PreToolUse hook refusing a mismatched verify-script invocation, mirroring E-1226's hook for `sqlite3 .endless` paths. It refuses earlier and can teach at the point of the mistake. But it is harness-specific per E-1962 and does not cover a human at a shell, so it cannot carry the rule alone.

## PRODUCT note

Nothing here is Endless-specific. Any project using Endless accumulates per-task verify scripts with the same property: they are gates for one task at one moment, they look like a regression suite, and they rot. The guard belongs in the shipped scaffolding, not in this repo's scripts only. `self_dev` changes nothing — the worktree-to-task lookup is the same call in both modes.

# Addendum — a bulk sweep, and why hermeticism is not an available fix (E-2071, 2026-08-26)

## What happened

Escalation from the single wrong script this task was filed on: a session ran
EVERY script — `for f in tests/tasks/*.sh` — 197 of them, as a "project-wide
regression check" before handing off. The rationalization was not "the rule does
not apply"; it was that running the suite is what you do before you hand work
over, and these live under `tests/`.

`e-1202-verify.sh` drives the real hook binary with a synthetic payload carrying
`session_id: "e1202-verify"`. The hook did what it always does: wrote a sessions
row into the MAIN database and bound it to the caller's live tmux pane. Two
session identities then claimed one pane, and `_resolve_companion` refuses an
ambiguous sibling set — so `esu` and every companion-resolving command stopped
working in Mike's shell for the rest of the session. The row is still there;
ending it needs a hand-driven SessionEnd.

## The finding that changes the mitigation set

`cmd/endless-go/main.go` PinMainDB's the `hook` and `tmux` subcommands
UNCONDITIONALLY — an explicit `--config-dir` is honored, but hook traffic is
otherwise pinned to main regardless of cwd or XDG_CONFIG_HOME, by design
(E-1450/E-1429: a fired hook is real-world activity in the real database).

So for any verify script that exercises hook behavior, "make it hermetic" is not
on the table in the usual way. The newer scripts' isolation pattern — a throwaway
config dir under the cache sandbox root, CLI run from outside the repo — does not
contain a hook invocation unless the script also threads `--config-dir` into it,
which the older ones do not and which is easy to omit silently.

This strengthens the case that the REFUSAL is the load-bearing defense, not
containment. A script that cannot run outside its own worktree cannot pollute
anything, whatever it does internally.

## Location, as a complement

The guard is the fix. But `tests/tasks/` is what makes the mistake reachable:
the scripts are shelved beside a real suite, `just test` runs `tests/`, and any
glob over `tests/` sweeps them in. Whatever the guard's final shape, consider
whether these belong under a path that does not read as a suite — cheap, and it
removes the invitation rather than only refusing it. (Filed separately as E-2077,
declined as a duplicate of this task; recorded here so the option is not lost.)

# Evidence: worktree-pinned hook binaries

All measured 2026-08-13 during one incident that started as "a resumed session
is invisible" and ended as "session writes are broken machine-wide."

## How the pin works, and why

Each worktree's `.claude/settings.json` points every Claude hook at that
worktree's own `bin/endless-go`. That is E-998, "Add per-worktree
`.claude/settings.json` so spawned sessions test the worktree's hook" — landed
2026-05-02 (`564ce2b`), still `unverified`. Its rationale: the alternative was
repointing the global symlink, "which puts every other live Claude session on
the machine on the unverified build for the duration of the swap."

That reasoning holds for an ACTIVE worktree carrying candidate hook code. It
does not hold for a worktree whose branch has fallen behind, where there is no
candidate worth verifying and the pin only costs.

E-998 is not to be reopened — it shipped, and this changes its mechanism rather
than completing it. It stays as the record of why the pin exists.

## Failure 1 — the binary dies, and the session runs untracked

`session goto 1808 --resume` opened a live Claude session that endless could not
see: sibling panes could not resolve it, and its DB row still read
`state=ended`, `process=''`. Its binary was built Jul 29. Run read-only:

    resolve project: task_types integrity check: tasktype: id=1 slug mismatch:
      enum="task", table="todo"

That is E-1659's `task`→`todo` rename. The check aborts the process before it
does anything, so SessionStart never registers the pane — and the error goes to
hook stderr, which nobody reads. The session then runs untracked for its whole
life.

## Failure 2 — the same binary corrupts the SHARED ledger

Later the same day, every session began failing on:

    upsert session: SQL logic error: no such column: NEW.process

Chain, verified:

- `internal/schema/schema.go` EMBEDS `schema.sql` into every binary, and the
  pre-rename `schema.sql` (at `38aa359e^`) declares two triggers,
  `sessions_null_process_on_end_update` and `..._insert`.
- E-1898 renamed `sessions.process` to `process_id` and its change file drops
  both triggers before `ALTER TABLE sessions DROP COLUMN process`. That
  migration was CORRECT and is marked applied — SQLite refuses DROP COLUMN
  while a trigger references the column, so the column being gone proves the
  drops ran.
- A stale binary's schema-ensure then re-created both triggers via
  `CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS`, against a table that no longer has the column
  they reference. Every session insert or state update failed from then on.

So a stale worktree binary is not merely self-harming. It writes damage into the
shared database that breaks every OTHER session on the machine. One dormant
worktree resumed after two weeks took down session writes for everyone.

## Scale, measured

    worktrees:                          135
    settings pinned to own binary:       89
    worktree binaries present:          103
    of those, containing pre-Aug-10 schema:  99   (96%)

Five of the 99 held LIVE sessions at the time — e-1901, e-1941, e-1919, e-1917,
e-1889 — so the corruption was ongoing, not latent. Remediated by copying main's
binary into all 99 and re-dropping the triggers; verified 103/103 current, 0
triggers, and session upserts landing again.

## Two measurement traps, both of which caught this session

**Timestamps are worthless.** e-1808's binary was timestamped 13:24 today and
contained Jul 29 code: `just build` had run WITHOUT the rebase, so the mtime
refreshed while the source did not. A freshness check based on mtime would have
passed that binary and delegated straight into the failure.

**The only reliable test is content.** `strings <binary> | grep -c process_id`
separated the 99 from the 4 in one pass. Whatever E-1972 chooses, the
compatibility signal must be derived from what the binary CONTAINS — an embedded
schema/enum fingerprint it can report — not from file metadata or branch
freshness heuristics.

**And it must run at hook time, on every event.** This session's own worktree
was compatible when created and went stale underneath a live session, with no
event marking the transition. A check performed once at worktree creation would
not have caught it.

## The loud-failure invariant, restated (Mike)

Inverting the hook binary is NOT a reversal of E-1662. The rule stands: when an
invariant fails, it fails loudly. What changes is which condition is the
invariant:

    If delegation determines the event should go to the worktree binary and that
    binary is absent or incompatible, THAT is the invariant violation and it
    fails loudly.

When delegation determines main's binary should handle the event, there is no
invariant to violate — main just handles it. So the inversion does not weaken
E-1662; it supplies the precondition it was always missing, because absence only
matters once something has decided the worktree binary was required.

Corollary: the delegation decision must be explicit and inspectable, since it is
now what determines whether an absent binary is an error or a non-event.

## The shape Mike proposed

Hooks always invoke main's known-good binary, which delegates to the worktree's
only when that one is verified compatible. Under the pin, the candidate binary
is the ONLY thing that runs, so when it breaks there is nothing alive to report
the fact — which is exactly why both failures above were silent. Inverting means
something working always starts.

Stated cost: the dispatch path in main's binary that runs BEFORE delegation is
never exercised as candidate code. Small and fixed; everything after the
delegation point is still candidate.

Open, and the reason this is a brainstorm rather than an implementation task:
what should drive the delegation decision. Mike: "delegation needs to be more
intelligent than opt-in vs. automatic."

## Absorbed: E-1704 and E-2038 (folded here 2026-08-23, both obsoleted)

Two tasks were obsoleted into this brainstorm rather than left to be invalidated
by whatever it decides. Their content is below so the correct task and plan can
be filed FROM this decision instead of rewritten around it.

### From E-1704 — bare shell invocations (was: self-re-exec into the worktree build)

From a bare (non-Claude) tmux pane inside a self-dev worktree, `endless` (Python)
and bare `endless-go` silently run MAIN's code. Worktree changes cannot be

### From E-2038 — the compatibility test itself

The `e-2011-home-relative-project-paths` change file ran against the shared main

Worktree binaries built before that compare a raw absolute cwd against the new

Evidence: zero stray project rows before that timestamp, five after

114 of 156 worktrees held a binary older than the migration. This is the same
population this brainstorm measured on Aug 13 (103 of 135), and the same root
cause as the stale-binary hook abort — a worktree binary that cannot read
current state — reached by a different failure path.

**The proposed test, which is this brainstorm's "verified compatible":**
`_schema_version` names every applied change file, and a binary ships a known
set under `internal/schema/changes/`. Markers present in the DB that the binary
does not ship mean the DB is AHEAD of the binary. Refuse or decline to delegate.
Ahead-only — a binary shipping changes the DB lacks is every pre-land worktree
and must stay normal. Escape hatches (`db apply-change`, `db path`, `db backup`,
`rebuild-db`) must never be gated, or a refused binary cannot be recovered.

**Note the integrity-check abort this task already documents (a Jul 29 build
dying on the E-1659 `task`→`todo` check) is the same class:** stale binary,
current DB. A single compatibility gate should cover both, which is the argument
for deciding it here rather than in two tasks.

### Cleanup owed either way

Five stray project rows exist; `project unregister <name>`, ONE name per

tasks, 0 decisions, 0 sessions, 153 activity rows. Cleanup without the gate is

# Addendum — the land window (evidence from E-1969, 2026-08-25)

Filed as E-2061 before searching, which was the wrong move; obsoleted and folded
in here, where the area already has an owner. This is evidence and one
constraint, not a competing shape.

## What happened

E-1969 renamed `sessions.active_task_id` to `sessions.task_id`. Its land
succeeded, and immediately after "Landed E-1969 into main" a Claude hook logged
50 lines, one per worktree:

    endless-go hook: reap worktrees: .endless/worktrees/e-1203:
      query active sessions: SQL logic error: no such column: active_task_id (1)

Old binary, new database — the same disagreement this task exists to resolve,
reached from the other direction.

## Why the window exists

`worktree land` applies the branch's schema changes at Step 5.5, and the
Justfile refreshes the installed binary only AFTER `endless worktree land`
returns. Between those two moments the real DB is migrated and the installed
binary is not. `internal/hookcmd/claude.go` calls
`monitor.ReapWorktreesForProject` from five places; one of them fired inside
that window.

The order is not a mistake and cannot be fixed by reordering:

- E-1941 moved apply-change AFTER the ff-merge because applying before it left
  the DB migrated to a schema no installed binary understood — the 2026-08-10
  machine-wide freeze.
- It cannot move later: `_record_landing` runs the same binary against the real
  DB (E-1664, inverted).
- Refreshing the binary earlier only relocates the window; the new binary would
  then meet the un-migrated DB and fail on the same read.

## The constraint this puts on the chosen shape

"Hooks always invoke main's known-good binary, which delegates to the worktree's
only when that one is verified compatible" assumes main's binary is known-good.
For the seconds of a land it is not: main's IS the stale one. A compatibility
check derived from an embedded schema fingerprint — which this task already
requires, and rightly, over any mtime heuristic — will find BOTH binaries
incompatible during that window.

So the delegation decision needs a third answer beyond "use main's" and "fail
loudly because the worktree's is incompatible": what to do when neither binary
matches the DB. Two candidates, both consistent with the loud-failure invariant
(E-1662), and this is the open question rather than a recommendation:

- Treat mid-migration as a known, bounded state and skip rather than error —
  the hook paths already fail open, so a skip is a smaller change than it
  sounds, and the reaper's work is idempotent and retried on the next event.
- Treat it as loud but singular: report "DB is mid-migration" once, not once per
  worktree, so the operator sees one line instead of 50 and does not read a
  successful land as a failed one.

The read case is the benign half. The write case is not hypothetical — Failure 2
above is exactly it, a stale binary re-creating dropped triggers against
`sessions` and breaking session writes for every session on the machine. That
was E-1898's rename; E-1659's enum rename was the other. A rename is not a new
class of change here, it is the class that has already caused this twice.

## A comment to retract while you are here

`internal/schema/changes/e-1929-add-tasks-removed.go` states that the window
between schema application and the binary swap "is never entered in practice."
It is entered. That file is where later changes go to copy their ordering
reasoning from — E-1969's change file did exactly that — so the false claim
propagates until someone corrects it at the source.

# Addendum — a use-case for whatever shape is chosen (from E-2071, 2026-08-26)

Not a new failure mode, and not a request to widen this task. One constraint the
chosen shape should be checked against, recorded because it is easy to miss when
the framing is "which binary runs".

## The constraint

`cmd/endless-go/main.go` PinMainDB's `hook` and `tmux` UNCONDITIONALLY. An
explicit `--config-dir` still wins (E-1429), but absent that, hook traffic goes
to the MAIN database regardless of cwd or XDG_CONFIG_HOME — deliberately, since
a fired hook is real-world activity in the real record.

This is the mechanism behind "Failure 2" above, stated as a general property
rather than as a schema-trigger story: **worktree hook traffic is never
contained.** It is not that a stale binary happened to reach the shared ledger;
nothing a worktree's hook does is confined to that worktree's sandbox. The
binary-selection question and the database-routing question look independent and
are not — whichever binary wins, its hook writes land in main.

## Why it turned up

A session drove `endless-go hook claude` with a synthetic payload while testing
something unrelated. It expected the surrounding sandbox isolation to contain it.
It did not: a sessions row was written into the main database and bound to a live
tmux pane, and every companion-resolving command then refused that pane as
ambiguous.

## What to check the chosen shape against

- If main's binary delegates to a worktree's, the delegate inherits the main pin.
  A "verified compatible" worktree binary is still writing to the shared record,
  so compatibility has to cover WRITE shapes (schema, event kinds), not just
  "does it start".
- If a compatibility probe runs the candidate binary, the probe must not itself
  be a hook invocation, or the probe writes to main as a side effect of asking
  whether it is safe to write to main.
- The loud-failure invariant stated above should extend to this: a worktree
  binary about to write to the shared record on behalf of a hook is worth saying
  out loud, since the blast radius is every session on the machine rather than
  the one worktree.

## Why prose is not enough

The rule already exists and is unambiguous. It was read, understood, paraphrased into "not required", and broken — by a session that could quote it. An agent's compliance with prose is negotiable at the moment it is inconvenient, which is precisely the moment enforcement has to exist.

## The load-bearing fix: guard inside the script

Each script already resolves its worktree root via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` in `main()`. Add a guard there: ask endless which task this worktree holds and exit 2 unless it matches the script's own id, with a refusal that names the sanctioned runners (`endless verify <id>`, `just verify <id>`) rather than just saying no.

Put it in a shared helper the scripts source, not copied into each — there are ~40 scripts and a copied guard is ~40 chances to omit it. Add it to whatever template new scripts are written from so one authored next month inherits it. Both sanctioned runners already know the task id, so they pass by construction.

This layer works for every user, every harness, and a human at a shell prompt.

Under prose-only rules that stale grep is a landmine: the next refactorer runs it, sees red, and "fixes" working code to match — which is exactly what happened here. Under the guard it is inert, because nobody outside E-1956's worktree can reach it. One cause, two symptoms, one task.

A PreToolUse hook refusing a mismatched verify-script invocation, mirroring E-1226's hook for `sqlite3 .endless` paths. It refuses earlier and can teach at the point of the mistake. But it is harness-specific per E-1962 and does not cover a human at a shell, so it cannot carry the rule alone.
